claim.why_it_matters: All sub-entry indentation on this page is lost, so sub-entries such as 'Exception checking 777' and 'infinite loop 686' read as free-standing top-level entries rather than as qualifiers of 'PERFORM statement'. Same systematic defect as pages 1249-1251.

verdict.reasoning:
Independently confirmed on both sides, but the claim's kind label is wrong and its severity is overstated.

PDF (rendered at 300 dpi, then cropped and upscaled 2x over the right column so the glyphs and the left edges of each line could be measured by eye): the index is printed with a two-level hierarchy. Reading the block verbatim, flush-left entries begin at one x-position and sub-entries at a clearly deeper one:
  'PERFORM phrase'            (flush)
      'EXIT statement  10, 623'   (indented)
  'PERFORM statemen'          (flush)
      'Exception-checkingt  706'  (indented)
  'PERFORM statement  682'    (flush)
      'Exception checking  777'   (indented)
      'Exception-checking  605, 613, 623, 638, 657, 675, 682,'  (indented)
              '691'               (deeper still - a wrapped continuation of the preceding line, not an entry)
      'infinite loop  686'        (indented)
  'PERFORM statement examples  1155'  (flush)
So the claim quotes the PDF accurately.

Markdown: verified against the CANONICAL specs/ISO_COBOL.md (lines 52303-52310), not merely the extracted slice, because page_workunit.py could in principle have stripped leading whitespace. It does not - slice_for() copies lines verbatim. The canonical file genuinely has every one of these lines flush-left with zero leading whitespace, matching the claim's quote exactly. The wrapped '691' is correctly rejoined onto its Exception-checking line, which is proper de-wrapping and not a defect.

So a real difference exists and it is not mere line wrapping or hyphenation: in a back-of-book index the indent is the only carrier of the parent/child relation, so 'infinite loop 686' standing flush-left reads as a top-level term rather than as 'PERFORM statement > infinite loop'. Meaning of the line changes, hence real=true.

What the claim gets wrong:
1. Kind 'misplaced-content' is inaccurate. Nothing is misplaced, transposed, re-ordered, or attached to the wrong parent. Every line, every page number, and the entire sequence match the print. The defect is a flattening - loss of the indent level - not a relocation of content.
2. Scope is far wider than 'this page' or 'the same as 1249-1251'. I counted leading-whitespace lines across the whole index region of the canonical markdown (lines 50722-53187, covering pages 1240 through 1260): ZERO indented lines out of 2465. The index was transcribed flush-left throughout. This is one systemic transcription convention, not a per-page defect, and it should be ledgered once for the index as a whole rather than as ~20 separate page findings.
3. Severity 'structural' overstates impact. No normative text is involved - this is the navigational index, every page reference is present and correct, and no rule, format diagram, or general rule is affected. Cosmetic/navigational.

Separately noted while reading the glyphs, and NOT a transcription error: the adjacent lines print in the PDF as 'PERFORM statemen' (no trailing t) and 'Exception-checkingt  706' (stray leading-word-final t). I read those glyphs directly at 2x zoom to be sure. That is a defect in the ISO print itself, and the markdown reproduces it faithfully.
verdict.corrected_description: Real, but mis-kinded and over-scoped. Not misplaced content: no line, page number, or ordering differs from the print. The actual defect is loss of index sub-entry INDENTATION - the PDF prints a two-level hierarchy ('PERFORM statement 682' flush, with 'Exception checking 777', 'Exception-checking 605, ..., 691' and 'infinite loop 686' indented beneath it), while the markdown renders all five lines flush-left, so the sub-entries read as free-standing top-level terms. This is systemic, not page-local: the canonical specs/ISO_COBOL.md has zero indented lines across the entire index (lines 50722-53187, pages 1240-1260), so it should be ledgered once as a single index-wide transcription convention rather than per page. Severity should be downgraded from structural to cosmetic/navigational - no normative rule text is affected and every page reference is intact. Unrelated to this finding, the neighbouring 'PERFORM statemen' / 'Exception-checkingt 706' oddity is a defect in the ISO print itself (verified by reading the printed glyphs at 2x) and is correctly reproduced by the markdown.
